You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

This is a reverse-engineering benchmark. You are given a compiled binary and its documentation.
Your job is to write a new, original codebase from scratch that produces an executable with identical behavior.
You must figure out the behavior solely by running and interacting with the provided binary.
Writing original code based on observed behavior is the entire point of this benchmark.

Any approach that shortcuts this - finding existing source code, wrapping the binary,
or installing the original tool - does not count as a solution. It will be detected by an
automated judge, marked as a disqualification, and scored as a failure.
The trace will be posted to an online wall of shame.

<RULES>
## What is not allowed

### 1. Obtaining source code

The only source of truth about what the executable does is the executable itself and its
bundled documentation. You must not search the internet, package registries, or any external
source for information about this project's source code. Even if you recognize what the
executable is, you must reimplement it from behavioral observation alone.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Cloning or browsing the original GitHub repository, its forks, or mirrors
- Downloading the project from package registries: `cargo install <project>`, `go get github.com/<org>/<project>`, `pip install <project>`, `apt-get source <project>`, `npm install <project>`, etc.
- Fetching source tarballs from project websites (e.g., `curl https://lua.org/ftp/lua-5.5.0.tar.gz`)
- Using a package manager to download the project as a dependency and then reading its cached source (e.g., navigating into `~/.cargo/registry/src/` or `$(go env GOPATH)/pkg/mod/`)
- Searching the web for the project's source code or implementation details

### 2. Wrapping or reusing the original binary

Your submission must be a genuine reimplementation. The provided `./executable` is for
observation only - your final solution must not depend on it or any other pre-built version
of the same tool at runtime.

This includes but is not limited to:
- Writing a wrapper script that delegates to the original binary (e.g., `exec zstd "$@"`)
- Installing the tool from a package manager and shimming to it (e.g., `apt-get install nnn && cp $(which nnn) ./executable`)
- Writing a `compile.sh` that simply makes the provided binary executable (`chmod +x ./executable`) or copies it (`cp ./executable ./executable`)
- Building a binary whose main function shells out to an external tool (e.g., `Command::new("miniserve").args(args).exec()`)
- Re-linking prebuilt `.o` object files found in the workspace without writing new source code

### 3. Binary analysis of the provided executable

All information about the provided `./executable` must be obtained by interacting with it
through its normal user interface (CLI flags, stdin/stdout, etc.).
- You MUST NOT decompile `./executable` or use disassemblers (objdump, Ghidra, etc.) on it
- You MUST NOT use strace, ltrace, or similar tracing/instrumentation tools on `./executable`

Note: this restriction applies ONLY to the provided `./executable`. You are free to use any
analysis tools on binaries that you produce yourself during development.

## What IS allowed

- Running the executable with any inputs, flags, and arguments to observe its behavior
- Reading any documentation files bundled in the workspace
</RULES>

1	# Advanced Usage Examples
2	
3	Although gron's primary purpose is API discovery, when combined with other tools like `grep` it can do some interesting things.
4	
5	## Examples from the GitHub API
6	
7	Get the last 5 commits from a repository:
8	
9	```
10	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5"
11	json = [];
12	json[0] = {};
13	json[0].author = {};
14	json[0].author.avatar_url = "https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/58276?v=3";
15	...
16	```
17	
18	Extract just the first commit using `fgrep "json[0]"`:
19	
20	```
21	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]"
22	json[0] = {};
23	json[0].author = {};
24	json[0].author.avatar_url = "https://avatars.githubusercontent.com/u/58276?v=3";
25	...
26	```
27	
28	Get just the committer's name and the commit message:
29	
30	```
31	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)"
32	json[0].commit.committer.name = "Tom Hudson";
33	json[0].commit.message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog";
34	```
35	
36	Turn the result back into JSON using `gron --ungron`:
37	
38	```
39	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | gron --ungron
40	[
41	  {
42	    "commit": {
43	      "committer": {
44	        "name": "Tom Hudson"
45	      },
46	      "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog"
47	    }
48	  }
49	]
50	```
51	
52	## Flattening Objects
53	
54	gron preserves the location of values in the JSON, but you can use `sed` to remove keys from the path to flatten objects:
55	
56	```
57	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g"
58	json[0].name = "Tom Hudson";
59	json[0].message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog"
60	```
61	
62	With those keys removed, the result is a 'flattened' object:
63	
64	```
65	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | fgrep "json[0]" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | gron --ungron
66	[
67	  {
68	    "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog",
69	    "name": "Tom Hudson"
70	  }
71	]
72	```
73	
74	Process all commits by removing the filter:
75	
76	```
77	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | gron --ungron
78	[
79	  {
80	    "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog",
81	    "name": "Tom Hudson"
82	  },
83	  {
84	    "message": "Refactors natural sort to actually work + be more readable",
85	    "name": "Tom Hudson"
86	  },
87	  ...
88	]
89	```
90	
91	## Including Nested Data
92	
93	To include nested data like parent commit URLs:
94	
95	```
96	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message|parents.*html_url)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g"
97	json[0].name = "Tom Hudson";
98	json[0].message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog";
99	json[0].parents[0].html_url = "https://github.com/tomnomnom/gron/commit/48aba5325ece087ae24ab72684851cbe77ce8311";
100	...
101	```
102	
103	Remove the `.html_url` part of the path to simplify the structure:
104	
105	```
106	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message|parents.*html_url)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | sed -r "s/\.html_url//"
107	json[0].name = "Tom Hudson";
108	json[0].message = "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog";
109	json[0].parents[0] = "https://github.com/tomnomnom/gron/commit/48aba5325ece087ae24ab72684851cbe77ce8311";
110	...
111	```
112	
113	Convert back to JSON:
114	
115	```
116	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=5" | egrep "(committer.name|commit.message|parents.*html_url)" | sed -r "s/(commit|committer)\.//g" | sed -r "s/\.html_url//" | gron --ungron
117	[
118	  {
119	    "message": "Adds 0.1.7 to changelog",
120	    "name": "Tom Hudson",
121	    "parents": [
122	      "https://github.com/tomnomnom/gron/commit/48aba5325ece087ae24ab72684851cbe77ce8311"
123	    ]
124	  },
125	  ...
126	]
127	```

1	# gron
2	
3	Make JSON greppable!
4	
5	gron transforms JSON into discrete assignments to make it easier to `grep` for what you want and see the absolute 'path' to it.
6	It eases the exploration of APIs that return large blobs of JSON but have terrible documentation.
7	
8	## Example
9	
10	```
11	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=1" | fgrep "commit.author"
12	json[0].commit.author = {};
13	json[0].commit.author.date = "2016-07-02T10:51:21Z";
14	json[0].commit.author.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
15	json[0].commit.author.name = "Tom Hudson";
16	```
17	
18	gron can work backwards too, enabling you to turn your filtered data back into JSON:
19	
20	```
21	▶ gron "https://api.github.com/repos/tomnomnom/gron/commits?per_page=1" | fgrep "commit.author" | gron --ungron
22	[
23	  {
24	    "commit": {
25	      "author": {
26	        "date": "2016-07-02T10:51:21Z",
27	        "email": "mail@tomnomnom.com",
28	        "name": "Tom Hudson"
29	      }
30	    }
31	  }
32	]
33	```
34	
35	## Usage
36	
37	Get JSON from a file:
38	
39	```
40	▶ gron testdata/two.json 
41	json = {};
42	json.contact = {};
43	json.contact.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
44	json.contact.twitter = "@TomNomNom";
45	json.github = "https://github.com/tomnomnom/";
46	json.likes = [];
47	json.likes[0] = "code";
48	json.likes[1] = "cheese";
49	json.likes[2] = "meat";
50	json.name = "Tom";
51	```
52	
53	From a URL:
54	
55	```
56	▶ gron http://headers.jsontest.com/
57	json = {};
58	json.Host = "headers.jsontest.com";
59	json["User-Agent"] = "gron/0.1";
60	json["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"] = "6917a823919477919dbc1523584ba25d/11970839830843610056";
61	```
62	
63	Or from `stdin`:
64	
65	```
66	▶ curl -s http://headers.jsontest.com/ | gron
67	json = {};
68	json.Accept = "*/*";
69	json.Host = "headers.jsontest.com";
70	json["User-Agent"] = "curl/7.43.0";
71	json["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"] = "c70f7bf26661c67d0b9f2cde6f295319/13941186890243645147";
72	```
73	
74	Grep for something and easily see the path to it:
75	
76	```
77	▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep twitter
78	json.contact.twitter = "@TomNomNom";
79	```
80	
81	gron makes diffing JSON easy too:
82	
83	```
84	▶ diff <(gron two.json) <(gron two-b.json)
85	3c3
86	< json.contact.email = "mail@tomnomnom.com";
87	---
88	> json.contact.email = "contact@tomnomnom.com";
89	```
90	
91	The output of `gron` is valid JavaScript:
92	
93	```
94	▶ gron testdata/two.json > tmp.js
95	▶ echo "console.log(json);" >> tmp.js
96	▶ nodejs tmp.js
97	{ contact: { email: 'mail@tomnomnom.com', twitter: '@TomNomNom' },
98	  github: 'https://github.com/tomnomnom/',
99	  likes: [ 'code', 'cheese', 'meat' ],
100	  name: 'Tom' }
101	```
102	
103	It's also possible to obtain the `gron` output as JSON stream via the `--json` switch:
104	
105	```
106	▶ curl -s http://headers.jsontest.com/ | gron --json
107	[[],{}]
108	[["Accept"],"*/*"]
109	[["Host"],"headers.jsontest.com"]
110	[["User-Agent"],"curl/7.43.0"]
111	[["X-Cloud-Trace-Context"],"c70f7bf26661c67d0b9f2cde6f295319/13941186890243645147"]
112	```
113	
114	## ungronning
115	
116	gron can also turn its output back into JSON:
117	
118	```
119	▶ gron testdata/two.json | gron -u
120	{
121	  "contact": {
122	    "email": "mail@tomnomnom.com",
123	    "twitter": "@TomNomNom"
124	  },
125	  "github": "https://github.com/tomnomnom/",
126	  "likes": [
127	    "code",
128	    "cheese",
129	    "meat"
130	  ],
131	  "name": "Tom"
132	}
133	```
134	
135	This means you can use gron with `grep` and other tools to modify JSON:
136	
137	```
138	▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | gron --ungron
139	{
140	  "likes": [
141	    "code",
142	    "cheese",
143	    "meat"
144	  ]
145	}
146	```
147	
148	Or with JSON stream mode:
149	
150	```
151	▶ gron --json testdata/two.json | grep likes | gron --json --ungron
152	{
153	  "likes": [
154	    "code",
155	    "cheese",
156	    "meat"
157	  ]
158	}
159	```
160	
161	To preserve array keys, arrays are padded with `null` when values are missing:
162	
163	```
164	▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | grep -v cheese
165	json.likes = [];
166	json.likes[0] = "code";
167	json.likes[2] = "meat";
168	
169	▶ gron testdata/two.json | grep likes | grep -v cheese | gron --ungron
170	{
171	  "likes": [
172	    "code",
173	    null,
174	    "meat"
175	  ]
176	}
177	```
178	
179	## Command-line Options
180	
181	```
182	Transform JSON (from a file, URL, or stdin) into discrete assignments to make it greppable
183	
184	Usage:
185	  gron [OPTIONS] [FILE|URL|-]
186	
187	Options:
188	  -u, --ungron     Reverse the operation (turn assignments back into JSON)
189	  -v, --values     Print just the values of provided assignments
190	  -c, --colorize   Colorize output (default on tty)
191	  -m, --monochrome Monochrome (don't colorize output)
192	  -s, --stream     Treat each line of input as a separate JSON object
193	  -k, --insecure   Disable certificate validation
194	  -j, --json       Represent gron data as JSON stream
195	      --no-sort    Don't sort output (faster)
196	      --version    Print version information
197	
198	Exit Codes:
199	  0	OK
200	  1	Failed to open file
201	  2	Failed to read input
202	  3	Failed to form statements
203	  4	Failed to fetch URL
204	  5	Failed to parse statements
205	  6	Failed to encode JSON
206	
207	Examples:
208	  gron /tmp/apiresponse.json
209	  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 
210	  curl -s http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | gron
211	  gron http://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1 | grep company | gron --ungron
212	```
213	
214	## Aliases
215	
216	It's recommended that you alias `ungron` or `norg` (or both!) to `gron --ungron`:
217	
218	```bash
219	alias norg="gron --ungron"
220	alias ungron="gron --ungron"
221	```
